title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Solids, Liquids and Gases Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Explain the observable properties of solids, liquids and gases by modelling the motion and arrangement of particles (Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on solids, liquids and gases and the particle model: particle diagrams, why liquids pour, why gases spread and squash, and why air has mass. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Particles explain solids, liquids and gases.
key_sub: How close the particles are and how they move explains each state.
body_html:
How to think about it

All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving.

  • Solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot, so solids keep their shape.
  • Liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other, so liquids pour and take the shape of their container.
  • Gas: particles far apart and moving fast, so gases spread out and can be squashed. Gases still have mass.
Example

Why can water be poured but ice cannot?

ice particles are held in place

water particles slide past each other

Answer: water is a liquid

Example

A tyre is pumped up. What happens to the air particles?

more particles go in

they are pushed closer together

Answer: they are compressed

Common mistakes

  • Thinking gases have no mass.
  • Thinking particles in a solid do not move at all (they vibrate).
  • Drawing liquid particles far apart (they are close together, like a solid, but jumbled).

faq.a: It is the idea that all matter is made of tiny moving particles. How close they are and how they move explains whether something is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
Yes. A ball or tyre gets a little heavier when it is pumped full of air, and a full scuba tank weighs more than an empty one.

faq.q: Why can gases be squashed but liquids cannot?
faq.a: Gas particles have lots of space between them, so they can be pushed closer. Liquid particles are already touching, so liquids hardly squash at all.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps the same volume but changes shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which state of matter has a definite volume?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Which of these is a gas: chocolate (at room temperature), flour, milk or the air inside a football?
items.e: The air inside a football is a gas.

items.q: Is lemonade a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Lemonade is a liquid.

items.q: Which state of matter fills up the whole of any container it is in?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Is water a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Water is a liquid.

items.q: Which of these is a solid: flour, helium in a balloon, melted chocolate or water vapour?
items.e: Tiny solid grains pour, but each keeps its shape.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Is honey a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It flows slowly, but it flows and takes the shape of its container.

items.q: Which of these is a solid: a stone, honey, orange juice or water vapour?
items.e: A stone is a solid.

items.q: Is a glass marble a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: A glass marble is a solid.

items.q: Which of these is a solid: a stone, helium in a balloon, milk or the bubbles in a fizzy drink?
c: the bubbles in a fizzy drink
items.e: A stone is a solid.

items.q: Which state of matter flows and takes the shape of its container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: What is all matter made of?
c: tiny particles that are too small to see
items.e: Solids, liquids and gases are all made of particles.

items.q: Is milk a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Milk is a liquid.

items.q: Which state of matter can be held in your hand without a container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which state of matter has particles that are furthest apart?
items.e: Gas particles have lots of space between them.

items.q: Which of these is a gas: a glass marble, butter (from the fridge), shampoo or the bubbles in a fizzy drink?
c: the bubbles in a fizzy drink
items.e: The bubbles are carbon dioxide gas.

items.q: Which state of matter can be compressed (squashed into a smaller space) easily?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Why does honey flow more slowly than water?
c: Honey's particles do not slide past each other as easily.
items.e: Both are liquids, but they flow at different rates.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a liquid?
c: close together but able to slide past each other
packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
far apart and moving quickly in all directions
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in ice?
c: none of them: ice has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: What happens to particles when a solid is heated?
c: They vibrate faster and move further apart.
items.e: Heating gives the particles more energy.

items.q: In which state are the particles close together but able to slide past each other?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: What does diagram A show?
c: a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a solid: particles far apart and not moving
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in water in a glass?
c: none of them: water in a glass has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: What does diagram A show?
c: a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: A bike tyre is pumped up. Where do the extra air particles go?
c: They are squashed closer together inside the tyre.
items.e: Gases can be compressed.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
c: close together but able to slide past each other
packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
far apart and moving quickly in all directions
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in water in a glass?
c: none of them: water in a glass has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: Is sand a solid or a liquid?
c: a liquid, because it can be poured
a solid: each grain keeps its shape
items.e: Tiny solid grains can be poured, but each grain is solid.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in water vapour (steam)?
c: none of them: water vapour has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: What does diagram B show?
c: a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: Why does a gas spread through a whole room?
c: Gases are pulled by gravity to fill rooms.
Its particles move quickly in all directions with lots of space between them.
Gas particles are larger than solid particles.
items.e: This is why we can smell a barbecue from far away.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in water vapour (steam)?
c: none of them: water vapour has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: What does diagram C show?
c: a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: What does diagram A show?
c: a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: In which state are the particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in ice?
c: none of them: ice has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: In which state are the particles packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Air from a small balloon is let into a big empty box. What happens to the air?
c: It spreads out to fill the whole box.
items.e: Gases fill their container.

items.q: Gases can be squashed (compressed) easily. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are held in fixed places
the particles are close but can slide past each other
the particles are far apart and move freely
items.e: Particle model: gases, because the particles are far apart and move freely.

items.q: Why does a gas fill its whole container?
c: Its particles move freely and spread out.
items.e: Gas particles move quickly in every direction until they spread through the whole space. The particles themselves do not get bigger.

items.q: Gases spread out to fill any container. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are held in fixed places
the particles are close but can slide past each other
the particles are far apart and move freely
items.e: Particle model: gases, because the particles are far apart and move freely.

items.q: When ice melts into water, what happens to the particles?
c: They stay the same but start to slide past each other.
items.e: Melting does not make new particles. The same water particles just move more freely.

items.q: Which state of matter escapes from an open container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Why is it hard to squeeze a block of wood into a smaller size?
c: Its particles are too big to move.
Its particles are already packed close together.
items.e: In a solid the particles are already touching, so there is almost no empty space to push them into.

items.q: Water is poured from a tall glass into a flat dish. What happens to its volume?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume.

items.q: When water boils and turns into water vapour, the particles
c: move faster and spread far apart
items.e: Heating makes the particles move faster. In water vapour they are far apart, so you cannot see them.

items.q: Why does an 'empty' bottle pushed upside down into water not fill up with water?
c: It is full of air, which occupies space.
items.e: Air takes up space.

items.q: Which has a definite volume but no definite shape?
items.e: Oil is a liquid.

items.q: Why can a liquid be poured?
c: Its particles can slide past each other.
Its particles are very far apart.
Its particles do not move at all.
items.e: Liquid particles touch, but they are not locked in place. They slide past each other, so the liquid flows.

items.q: Which is the same in an ice cube and in a puddle of the same water?
c: how close the particles are in a pattern
items.e: Both are made of water particles. The ice has them locked in place, and the puddle lets them slide.

items.q: In which state of matter are the particles farthest apart?
c: They are the same distance apart in every state.
items.e: Gas particles are far apart. That is why a gas can be squeezed into a smaller space.

items.q: Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are held in fixed places
the particles are far apart and move freely
the particles are close but can slide past each other
items.e: Particle model: liquids, because the particles are close but can slide past each other.

items.q: Do the particles in a solid move?
c: Yes, they vibrate on the spot.
Yes, they move freely around the room.
Only when the solid is cold.
items.e: They vibrate but stay in place.

items.q: Solids can be held in your hand and do not flow. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are close but can slide past each other
the particles are far apart and move freely
the particles are held in fixed places
items.e: Particle model: solids, because the particles are held in fixed places.

items.q: A model of a solid should show particles that are
c: touching but sliding at the bottom only
items.e: Solid particles are packed tightly in a pattern and vibrate in place.

items.q: Liquids can be poured. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are close but can slide past each other
the particles are far apart and move freely
the particles are held in fixed places
items.e: Particle model: liquids, because the particles are close but can slide past each other.

items.q: Which states of matter cannot be squashed into a smaller space?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Why can a syringe of air be pushed in further than a syringe of water?
c: Air can be compressed; water cannot be compressed easily.
items.e: Gases have no definite volume.

items.q: A scientist says, “Everything around you is made of particles.” Which object is not included?
items.e: Light is energy, not matter, so it is not made of particles of matter.

items.q: An empty scuba tank has a mass of 15 kg. Filled with air pressed in tightly, it has a mass of 19 kg. Which conclusion is correct?
c: The tank itself gained 4 kg of metal.
The air inside has a mass of 4 kg.
The air inside has a mass of 19 kg.
items.e: 19 − 15 = 4 kg of air. Packing more air particles into the tank adds mass.

items.q: Mia weighed a flat football, then pumped air into it and weighed it again. What did Mia find?
items.e: Air has mass.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a use of the fact that gases can be compressed?
c: pumping air into a bicycle tyre
storing cooking gas in a cylinder
items.e: Compressed air or gas is stored in tyres and tanks.

items.q: Oliver weighs a sealed bottle of fizzy drink: 550 g. After opening it and letting the bubbles escape for a day, it weighs 549 g. How much mass of gas escaped?
items.e: 550 − 549 = 1 g. Gases have mass.

items.q: Which tool would help you show that air takes up space?
items.e: As you blow air into a balloon, the balloon gets bigger. The air takes up space inside it.

items.q: What is air made of?
c: a mixture of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen
items.e: About 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

items.q: You can smell garlic in a pan from 10 metres away, even though you cannot see anything moving through the air. What is the best explanation?
c: The smell is light that travels to your eyes.
Tiny particles from it spread through the air to your nose.
Smells are not made of anything.
The air in the room turns into the food.
items.e: Particles too small to see leave the source and spread out among the air particles until some reach your nose.

items.q: An empty scuba tank has a mass of 10 kg. Filled with air pressed in tightly, it has a mass of 16 kg. Which conclusion is correct?
c: The tank itself gained 6 kg of metal.
The air inside has a mass of 6 kg.
The air inside has a mass of 16 kg.
items.e: 16 − 10 = 6 kg of air. Packing more air particles into the tank adds mass.

items.q: Kai sealed the tip of a syringe filled with air and pushed the plunger. What happened?
c: The plunger could not move at all.
The air escaped through the plastic.
The plunger moved in a little, because air can be compressed.
items.e: Gases can be compressed.

items.q: Why can't you see the particles that make up a rock?
c: The particles are hidden inside a shell.
They are much too small to see.
Only liquids are made of particles.
items.e: Rocks, water and air are all made of particles. The particles are too small to see.

items.q: What is matter?
c: anything that has mass and takes up space
items.e: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Air is matter even though you cannot see it.

items.q: Which state of matter can be squashed easily?
items.e: Particles are far apart.

items.q: Why can you pour water but not a stone?
c: Liquid particles can slide past each other; solid particles are held in place.
items.e: Particles explain properties.

items.q: What are the three states of matter?
items.e: Everything is one of these.

items.q: Jack weighs a sealed bottle of fizzy drink: 520 g. After opening it and letting the bubbles escape for a day, it weighs 518 g. How much mass of gas escaped?
items.e: 520 − 518 = 2 g. Gases have mass.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
items.e: A solid keeps its shape. A liquid takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill it.

items.q: You can smell baking bread from 5 metres away, even though you cannot see anything moving through the air. What is the best explanation?
c: The air in the room turns into the food.
Tiny particles from it spread through the air to your nose.
The smell is light that travels to your eyes.
Smells are not made of anything.
items.e: Particles too small to see leave the source and spread out among the air particles until some reach your nose.

items.q: Do gases have mass?
c: Yes, they have mass even though we cannot see most of them.
items.e: An inflated ball weighs more than a flat one.

items.q: Water drops form on the outside of a cold glass of lemonade. Where did the water come from?
c: lemonade that leaked through the glass
nowhere: it was made from nothing
water vapour in the air that cooled and turned into liquid
items.e: The air has water vapour in it. When the vapour touches the cold glass, its particles slow down and join into drops (condensation).

items.q: A sponge gets smaller when squeezed. Does this mean solids can be squashed?
c: Yes, all solids can be squashed.
No. The air in the holes is squeezed out; the solid itself does not shrink.
items.e: Think about what is in the holes.

items.q: Kai wants to test which liquid flows fastest down a ramp. What should he keep the same?
c: only the colour of the liquids
the amount of each liquid, the ramp and its slope
items.e: Only the liquid should change.

items.q: Ella tests four liquids. Time to flow down a ramp: water 2 s, oil 6 s, honey 40 s, dishwashing liquid 15 s. Which flows most slowly?
items.e: The longest time means the slowest flow.

items.q: Why does a smell spread across a room?
c: Gas particles move and spread out in all directions.
Smells are not made of particles.
items.e: Gas particles move freely.

items.q: What does diagram B show?
c: a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: How could you show that a gas has mass?
c: Weigh a flat football, pump it up, and weigh it again.
items.e: More air, more mass.

items.q: What does diagram B show?
c: a solid: particles far apart and not moving
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: Noah wraps an ice cube in a bag, seals it and weighs it: 25 g. He weighs it again after it melts. What should the scale show?
items.e: Melting does not add or remove particles. The water has the same mass as the ice: 25 g.

items.q: A sealed bag of chips puffs up when it is taken up a high mountain. What is inside the bag that causes this?
items.e: The bag is full of gas particles. With less air pushing on the bag from outside, the gas inside spreads out more.

items.q: Priya wants to show that air has mass. Which investigation is best?
c: Weigh a flat ball, pump it up, then weigh it again.
Look at air with a hand lens.
Measure the temperature of the air.
Blow on her hand and feel it.
items.e: Comparing the mass before and after adding air shows that the air itself has mass.

items.q: A puddle dries up on a sunny day. Where did the water go?
c: It was destroyed by the sun.
Its particles went into the air as water vapour.
It soaked up into the clouds as a liquid at once.
items.e: Water evaporates: its particles leave the puddle and move into the air as a gas, too small to see.

items.q: Mia weighs a flat beach ball (150 g), then pumps it up and weighs it again. What will the scale most likely show?
items.e: Air has mass.

items.q: Ethan blows up two balloons the same size. He puts one in a warm room and one outside on a cold night. What happens to the outside balloon?
items.e: Cooling makes the air particles move more slowly and take up less space.

items.q: Ruby puts a drop of food colouring in hot water and in cold water. Which result is most likely?
c: It does not spread in either.
It spreads faster in the cold water.
It spreads faster in the hot water.
It spreads at the same rate.
items.e: Particles move faster in hot water.

items.q: Which question could be answered with a particle model?
c: Why does a gas spread to fill a room?
items.e: A particle model explains how matter behaves, like gas particles moving and spreading out.

items.q: Which observation is evidence that air takes up space?
c: A cup pushed upside down into water stays dry inside.
items.e: The air trapped in the cup keeps the water out. Two things cannot take up the same space.

items.q: Harper puts a balloon on the neck of a bottle and moves the bottle from hot water into ice water. What happens to the balloon?
c: It shrinks, because the air particles slow down and move closer together.
items.e: Cooling slows the particles, so the air takes up less space and the balloon goes flat.

items.q: How could you show that air takes up space?
c: Push an upside-down cup into water: the air stops the water filling it.
items.e: Gases take up space.

items.q: Using Ella's results, which list orders the liquids from fastest to slowest?
items.e: Shorter times mean faster flow.
